<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span>: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Guy Dar
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">guy.dar@cs.tau.ac.il</span></a>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Independent Researcher
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We build upon <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, a procedure designed to align embedding spaces without parallel data. While it usually finds a near-perfect alignment, it is expensive and unstable. We present <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span>, a simple and efficient alternative that is highly robust and incurs a much lower computational cost. Moreover, the transformation that <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> learns is <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">linear</span>. The method consists of three main stages: a tentative matching of pseudo-parallel embedding vectors, transformation fitting, and iterative refinement. Our linear alternative exceeds the original instantiation of <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> by orders of magnitude in efficiency, while matching or exceeding its alignment performance. The method’s stability and interpretable steps facilitate scaling and unlock new opportunities for adoption in new domains and fields.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><a href="https://github.com/guy-dar/mini-vec2vec" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">

<span class="ltx_inline-block fas fa-github" aria-hidden="true">
</span><span class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter"> github.com/guy-dar/mini-vec2vec</span>
</a></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Text embeddings, also called sentence embeddings, represent chunks of text in a high-dimensional vector space. They capture complex linguistic relationships and enable downstream tasks, such as semantic similarity and information retrieval. Naturally, different embedding models induce incompatible embedding spaces that cannot be compared directly, due to differences in architecture or initialization. The output of one model looks like gibberish to another.
This can be easily solved with supervised training – the translation between embedding models can be learned from embedding pairs representing the same sentences. However, the unsupervised problem, where we don’t have access to parallel embeddings of the same sentences, is much harder.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The unsupervised alignment of <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">word</span> embeddings has been studied extensively for a long time, often for the practical goal of aligning monolingual word embeddings from different languages. However, <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">text</span> embeddings have been mostly ignored. With the increasing popularity of databases of text embeddings, leakage of sensitive vector data becomes a real possibility. It has been shown that embedding inversion methods can extract the texts from the vectors alone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song and Raghunathan, 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Morris et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, but they require access to the model. Unsupervised alignment can be used to extend the attack to unknown proprietary models. The attacker just translates the embeddings to a known space and applies inversion methods on the translated embeddings – extracting the text from the data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite> have proposed <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, a method based on CycleGAN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2017</a>)</cite> for fully unsupervised text embedding alignment. As the logic behind their method, they cite a principle sometimes called <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Universal Geometry</span> or the <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Platonic Representation Hypothesis</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which posits that well-trained representations, regardless of architectures or initialization, tend to converge toward <span id="S1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">geometrically</span> similar spaces. This means that there is a way to rotate one embedding space to make it compatible with the other, and vice versa.
While <span id="S1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> is successful in finding a good alignment, the use of adversarial training is computationally intensive, requires careful hyperparameter tuning, and is subject to training instabilities like mode collapse, oscillatory behavior, or failure to converge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saxena and Cao, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow, 2017</a>)</cite>. Moreover, adversarial methods typically demand substantial computational resources, including GPU acceleration and large amounts of training data – factors that may prohibit their utilization by most researchers and users.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We hypothesize that the transformation between the embedding spaces is of a simple form (linear, specifically), and that it can be learned without adversarial methods. Indeed, in word embedding alignment much of the work has focused on this setup as well <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grave et al., 2019</a>, <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">inter alia</span>)</cite>. To achieve a similar goal in sentence embeddings, <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> seeks to identify signals of similarities in the geometric structure of sentence embedding spaces. We propose a very simple pipeline (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for a schematic overview), which consists of three steps:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Approximate Matching</span>: We match, in an unsupervised way, a small set of artificial pairs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Initial Transformation</span>: We find a linear map between the pairs and apply it to the full data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Iterative Refinement</span>: We then iteratively apply the operator, match each embedding to the closest embeddings in the other space, and learn a new operator on top of this matching.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S1.p4.2" class="ltx_p">This pipeline resembles some methods from unsupervised word embedding alignment – but text embeddings are somewhat different from word embeddings, so they require other tricks to make it work. Perhaps the most significant difference is the Approximate Matching method we rely on. At a high level, we need to find a new way to identify stable central landmarks and match them between sentence embedding spaces. Methods in word alignment implicitly rely on word vocabularies, which have special features (e.g., common words between languages, word frequencies, distributional properties of words, etc.). On the other hand, sentence embeddings can be seen as sparse samples from an “infinite” vocabulary, rendering them closer to, for instance, image embeddings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">After we have found an approximate match, the differences between word and sentence embeddings blur, and similar methods can be applied. We have developed the pipeline unaware of existing literature, so it is possible that our design decisions presented here are suboptimal or less common. Having said that, even in the Initial Alignment and Iterative Refinement steps, the design caters to specific characteristics uncommon in word embeddings, or at least less salient. For instance, when matching embeddings to their nearest neighbors, we average multiple nearest neighbors because there is no one-to-one matching between data points. This is often not the case in word alignment, since most languages, even if they are very distant, rely on closed vocabularies that significantly overlap.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We find <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> offers several key advantages: computational efficiency (very fast and runs on a commodity CPU), training stability (good performance and robust to hyperparameters), interpretability (each step has a clear geometric interpretation), and sample efficiency (60k vs 2 million samples). Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate that this simple approach <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">not only matches but often exceeds</span> the performance of the more complex adversarial method while requiring <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">orders of magnitude less computational resources</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2510.02348v4/mini-pipeline.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:543/141;" width="543" height="141" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">A simplified illustration of the <span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> pipeline.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The hypothesis that neural networks converge to geometrically similar representations has been explored across multiple domains and scales. Early work by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah (2015)</a></cite> has revealed striking structural similarities in representations of different convolutional networks, suggesting that the geometric organization of learned features might be more universal than previously assumed. The <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Platonic Representation Hypothesis</span>, formally articulated by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al. (2024)</a></cite>, represents the most comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding Universal Geometry.
The hypothesis posits that well-trained representations converge toward a shared geometric structure that reflects the underlying structure of the data domain.
This means that distances (and similarities) between objects should be roughly independent of the embedding model. For example, to compute the semantic similarity between <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“I love your dog”</span> and <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“I love my cat”</span>, we would use cosine similarity between their embeddings. According to Universal Geometry, the answer should (theoretically) have little dependence on the model used. This makes sense intuitively, as <span id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">semantic</span> similarity originates from <span id="S2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">semantic</span> meaning. It is a fundamentally linguistic concept learned from the data itself.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Relative Representations</h4>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moschella et al. (2022)</a></cite> have operationalized the observations of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah (2015)</a></cite> and proposed to use relative representations as a mathematically principled framework for comparing latent spaces. While absolute coordinates vary arbitrarily across models, we know now that relative information, like similarity between two objects, is (approximately) agnostic to the choice of embedding model. They propose to choose an agreed-upon set of data points, called anchors, that other data points will be compared to, and use them like landmarks on a map. In order to specify the location of a point, we specify how close it is to every landmark. If we have enough anchors and they are sufficiently diverse, we can “geo-locate” the point by its relative position alone. Since it requires a small set of paired anchors, the method cannot operate as-is in a fully unsupervised manner.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Denote the set of possible data points by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> (e.g., sentences, images, or any other modality; note these are abstract objects and not their vector representations) and the embedding function by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E:\mathcal{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given a set of anchor data points <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A=\{\mathbf{a}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>⊆</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A=\{\mathbf{a}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\subseteq\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>, the <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">relative representation</span> of <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math> under anchors <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and embedding <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> is the vector:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{A,E}(\mathbf{z})=[\,\operatorname{sim}(E(\mathbf{z)},E(\mathbf{a}_{1})),\,\operatorname{sim}(E(\mathbf{z}),E(\mathbf{a}_{2})),\,\ldots,\,\operatorname{sim}(E(\mathbf{z}),E(\mathbf{a}_{k}))\,]," <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>sim</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is a similarity function (typically cosine similarity).
For two embedding models satisfying the Universal Geometry assumption, relative representations of the same data point are roughly the same, i.e., <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}_{A,E_{1}}(\mathbf{z})\approx\mathbf{r}_{A,E_{2}}(\mathbf{z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}_{A,E_{1}}(\mathbf{z})\approx\mathbf{r}_{A,E_{2}}(\mathbf{z})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methodology</h2>

<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Problem Formulation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the setup laid out in <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, let <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}_{A}=\{\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{A}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}_{A}=\{\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n_{A}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{X}_{B}=\{\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{B}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒳</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{X}_{B}=\{\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n_{B}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote two sets of <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional embeddings. The sentences that created these embeddings are drawn from a shared underlying distribution <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, but all sentences are different and there is <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">no overlap</span> between the two datasets. We organize the embeddings into matrices <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{X}_{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{A}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{X}_{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{A}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{X}_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{B}\times d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{X}_{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{B}\times d}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each row corresponds to a single embedding vector.
Our goal is to learn a transformation function <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(E_{A}(\mathbf{z}))\approx E_{B}(\mathbf{z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(E_{A}(\mathbf{z}))\approx E_{B}(\mathbf{z})</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐳</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}</annotation></semantics></math> represents a data point <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐳</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒵</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{z}\in\mathcal{Z}</annotation></semantics></math>. More generally, the setup described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite> allows for learning a pair of functions <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{A},f_{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{A},f_{B}</annotation></semantics></math> sending embeddings to a third space, such that <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{A}(E_{A}(\mathbf{z}))\approx f_{B}(E_{B}(\mathbf{z}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐳</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{A}(E_{A}(\mathbf{z}))\approx f_{B}(E_{B}(\mathbf{z}))</annotation></semantics></math>, but we will not take advantage of this flexibility here.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Motivation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we restrict our attention to linear transformations. Further, we constrain the search space to orthogonal transformations, i.e., matrices <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> that satisfy <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{T}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐈</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{T}=\mathbf{W}^{T}\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{I}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is motivated by the Universal Geometry hypothesis – we expect distances and similarities to be preserved by the transformation. In practice, we later relax this assumption and use an exponentially-smoothed average of orthogonal matrices to enforce orthogonality softly.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> resembles many approaches in unsupervised word embedding alignment. It proceeds in three main stages: approximate matching, transformation fitting, and iterative refinement. Unfortunately, text embeddings are somewhat more complicated than word embeddings, partly because they are non-overlapping – there is no small exhaustive set (a vocabulary) of objects that need to be matched. The very concept of non-overlapping datasets is somewhat contrived for word embeddings, precisely because the set of possible objects is closed and relatively small. Even in multilingual matching, words mostly have a ground-truth one-to-one match.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond the overlap between the datasets, most works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf, 2018</a>)</cite> rely on the statistics of words or other word-specific features (for finding a seed dictionary). Optimal transport-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grave et al., 2019</a>)</cite> rely heavily on matching points between the sets (often one-to-one, but this can be alleviated), and they become computationally intensive. Theoretically speaking, in a non-overlapping dataset, OT could find sentences that are (only) similar and match them to one another, and then a parametric mapping could be learned on top of them (a methodology similar to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grave et al. (2019)</a></cite>, only applied to non-overlapping data). In practice, when <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite> have compared their method to multiple OT methods, <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">in an oracle setup</span>, they didn’t work better than <span id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">the most naive baseline</span>, indicating that even in the oracle setup, and even as a first step for learning a mapping, they are insufficient.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We will now proceed to describe our algorithm in detail (pseudo-code is provided in Listing <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="LST1" class="ltx_figure ltx_lstlisting ltx_align_center">

<div id="lstnumberx9" class="ltx_listingline">

<div id="lstnumberx10" class="ltx_listingline"><span id="lstnumberx10.1" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">    </span><span id="lstnumberx10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_keyword ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;--ltx-fg-color:#FF00FF;">return</span><span id="lstnumberx10.3" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">W</span>
</div>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Preprocessing</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first normalize the embeddings in both spaces. We center each set around its respective mean and normalize the embeddings to the unit hypersphere:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{A}}\mathbf{X}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}=\mathbf{X}_{A}-\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐗</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{A}}\mathbf{X}_{A}^{T}\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}},\quad\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}=\mathbf{X}_{A}-\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>A</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]\|_{2}},\quad\text{similarly for space }B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐗</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mtext>similarly for space </mtext><mi>B</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]}{\|\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{A}[i,:]\|_{2}},\quad\text{similarly for space }B</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{A}</annotation></semantics></math> is the mean of space <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{1}_{n_{A}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the vector of ones of length <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\cdot\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\cdot\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is the L2 norm.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Approximate Matching</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To find an approximate matching, a small seed of pairs of (approximate) matches, we need to find stable landmarks that are likely to exist in both spaces, despite the non-overlapping data. The natural candidates are clusters. We conjecture that clusters represent recurring themes between the datasets and, therefore, should be consistent between the datasets. But even if we find the same set of clusters in both spaces exactly, we still need to match each cluster (centroid) to its corresponding cluster (centroid) in the other space. To match the clusters, we rely on pairwise similarities, conjecturing they encode enough information to identify the matching uniquely (this intuition is shared with Gromov-Wasserstein <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mémoli, 2011</a>)</cite>). We match the clusters based on similarity matrices, with Quadratic Assignment Problem (QAP) solvers. These assumptions are not trivial, but the method works relatively well as-is, though often requiring a few attempts due to the stochasticity and sensitivity of the clustering and matching algorithms. To mitigate this, we run cluster-and-match multiple times and ensemble the results. We will now describe a single run, and then explain how we robustify it by ensembling.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Centroid Matching</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform k-means clustering in each embedding space independently and obtain cluster centroids <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j}\}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j=1,\ldots,C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j=1,\ldots,C</annotation></semantics></math>. We then compute pairwise similarities in each space:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S^{A}_{ij}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S^{A}_{ij}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}),\quad S^{B}_{ij}=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{j}),\quad S^{B}_{ij}=\cos(\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{c}^{B}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> are the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th cluster centroids in spaces <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We then find the optimal matching between the cluster centroids by solving the <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Quadratic Assignment Problem</span> (QAP), which finds a permutation that aligns the similarity matrices optimally:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{C}}\;\sum_{i=1}^{C}\sum_{j=1}^{C}S^{A}_{ij}\,S^{B}_{\pi(i)\,\pi(j)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>π</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>C</mi></msub></mrow></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>C</mi></munderover><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{C}}\;\sum_{i=1}^{C}\sum_{j=1}^{C}S^{A}_{ij}\,S^{B}_{\pi(i)\,\pi(j)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi:\{1,2,...,C\}\rightarrow\{1,2,...,C\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi:\{1,2,...,C\}\rightarrow\{1,2,...,C\}</annotation></semantics></math> is a permutation from the set <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>C</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{C}</annotation></semantics></math> of all permutations on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> elements. Due to the small number of cluster centroids, this takes only a few seconds. Conceptually, we can think of QAP in terms of cosine similarity, where we want to find the permutation that will maximize the cosine similarity between the (flattened) similarity matrices.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Option 1: Relative Representations</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Once we have identified an alignment between <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A\text{-}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A\text{-}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B\text{-centroids}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>-centroids</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B\text{-centroids}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use the aligned centroids as anchors. We represent each embedding through its relationships to anchor points. For embedding <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{C})]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{C})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Similarly, for <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute (note that we need to re-arrange the indices with <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>π</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi</annotation></semantics></math>):</p>
<table id="S3.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{B}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(1)}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(2)}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(C)})]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{B}_{i}=[\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(1)}),\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(2)}),\ldots,\cos(\mathbf{x}^{B}_{i},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(C)})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Option 2: Alternative Approach</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Curiously, we have found that it is possible to sidestep relative representations. Instead, it is possible to use the aligned centroids directly.</p>
<table id="S3.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{c}^{A}_{C}];\qquad\mathbf{r}^{B}_{i}=[\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(1)},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(2)},\ldots,\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(C)}]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mi>C</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">;</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐜</mi><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>B</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{c}^{A}_{1},\mathbf{c}^{A}_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{c}^{A}_{C}];\qquad\mathbf{r}^{B}_{i}=[\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(1)},\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(2)},\ldots,\mathbf{c}^{B}_{\pi(C)}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While the relative representations method learns from information derived from the entire data, the centroid-only approach requires just the centroids themselves.
Both methods are efficient, and this simplified method is only slightly more efficient. It seems to do worse after the Initial Transformation step (Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Initial Transformation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), but it converges normally in the Iterative Refinement steps (Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Iterative Refinement ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a>). We emphasize that we haven’t tested it as thoroughly as the relative representation approach. For future reference, we call this variant <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">“<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> centroid-only”</span>. Note that the centroid-only method is also much closer in spirit to many of the alignment methods discussed above that find a seed dictionary matching (the centroids here) and build on that. In this paper, we will <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">not focus</span> on this variant and discuss it here only for completeness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustification via Ensembling</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We improve robustness by repeating the process described above and concatenating relative representations from multiple runs:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,1};\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,2};\ldots;\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,s}]\in\mathbb{R}^{sC},\qquad\text{similarly for space }B" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mtext>similarly for space </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>B</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}=[\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,1};\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,2};\ldots;\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i,s}]\in\mathbb{R}^{sC},\qquad\text{similarly for space }B</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This concatenation creates richer structural signatures that are more robust to the noise that comes from bad alignments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Initial Transformation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct pseudo-parallel pairs by sending each element in space <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> to the average of its <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors from space <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> (based on similarity in relative space):</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{C}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\frac{1}{k}\hskip-3.00003pt\sum_{\tiny\hskip 2.94443pt{\mathbf{r}^{B}_{j}\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})}\hskip-13.25018pt}\hskip-3.00003pt\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\,\,\,\,\right):\,i=1,\ldots,n_{A}\right\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></mfrac><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.710em">𝐫</mi><mi mathsize="0.720em">j</mi><mi mathsize="0.720em">B</mi></msubsup><mo mathsize="0.710em">∈</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.710em">𝒩</mi><mi mathsize="0.720em">k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.710em" minsize="0.710em">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathsize="0.710em">𝐫</mi><mi mathsize="0.720em">i</mi><mi mathsize="0.720em">A</mi></msubsup><mo maxsize="0.710em" minsize="0.710em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>B</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.278em">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.448em">:</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}=\left\{\left(\mathbf{x}^{A}_{i},\frac{1}{k}\hskip-3.00003pt\sum_{\tiny\hskip 2.94443pt{\mathbf{r}^{B}_{j}\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})}\hskip-13.25018pt}\hskip-3.00003pt\mathbf{x}^{B}_{j}\,\,\,\,\right):\,i=1,\ldots,n_{A}\right\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}_{k}(\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors to <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐫</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>A</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{r}^{A}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the concatenated relative representation space. Note that the neighborhood information is obtained from the relative space (which is shared) and averaging takes place in the absolute space <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>. Optimal orthogonal transformation is obtained by Procrustes analysis: <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{*}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>𝐕𝐔</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{*}=\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{T}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{B})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐔</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝚺</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐕</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>SVD</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐀</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐁</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{U}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\mathbf{V}^{T}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{B})</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐀</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> are matrices formed from the pseudo-parallel pairs in <math id="S3.SS3.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Iterative Refinement</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The initial transformation provides a coarse alignment that we refine with two complementary strategies. Pseudo-code is provided in Listing <span class="ltx_ref ltx_missing_label ltx_ref_self"></span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refine-1: Matching-based Refinement</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This refinement strategy proceeds by transforming embeddings from space <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> using <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math>, averaging their nearest neighbors in space <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>, and obtaining a new orthogonal transformation with Procrustes analysis – similar to the process described in the Initial Transformation stage (Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Initial Transformation ‣ 3 Methodology ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a>), with the crucial difference that now the similarity is computed in the ambient space <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> rather than relative space. This technique is also present in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf (2018)</a></cite>, and it is often called <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Iterative Closest Point</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Besl and McKay, 1992</a>, ICP;)</cite>. A minor difference is that we average multiple points rather than relying on a single neighbor. As mentioned above, this is due to our no-overlap setup. Since ICP is cheap, we run it for many iterations (50–100), using subsampling to boost computational efficiency further.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use exponential smoothing for transformation updates:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{(t+1)}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{W}^{(t)}+\alpha\mathbf{W}_{\text{new}}^{(t)}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext>new</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{(t+1)}=(1-\alpha)\mathbf{W}^{(t)}+\alpha\mathbf{W}_{\text{new}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Refine-2: Clustering-based Refinement</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This strategy aims to improve the large-scale matching between the spaces. We begin by clustering the embeddings in space <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>. We then apply <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> to the cluster centroids and cluster the <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> embeddings, where the clustering algorithm is initialized with the transformed <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> centroids as the initial centroids. The transformed clusters should be close to a set of clusters in the new space. We therefore expect the clustering algorithm to make only minor adjustments, correcting biases in the transformation and moving the centroids to their “right positions” in space <math id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>. We expect the pseudo-parallel pairs based on cluster assignments to be more robust than individual nearest neighbors used in Refine-1. Similar to the first refinement strategy, we use exponential smoothing.
Crucially, we find that <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">one</span> iteration of Refine-2 improves the alignment obtained by Refine-1. Two or more lead to a slight deterioration of the alignment. We conjecture that the ICP procedure might have introduced systematic bias that requires correction, but after this correction, the clustering-based refinement does not contribute, and only dilutes the signal.</p>
</div>
<figure id="LST2" class="ltx_figure ltx_lstlisting ltx_align_center">
<div id="LST2.2" class="ltx_listing ltx_lst_language_Python ltx_lstlisting ltx_listing"><div class="ltx_listing_data"><a href="data:text/plain;base64," download="">⬇</a></div>
