</span><span id="lstnumberx48.13" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">W</span><span id="lstnumberx48.14" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx48.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">+</span><span id="lstnumberx48.16" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx48.17" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">alpha</span><span id="lstnumberx48.18" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx48.19" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">*</span><span id="lstnumberx48.20" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_space ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;"> </span><span id="lstnumberx48.21" class="ltx_text ltx_lst_identifier ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:70%;">W_new</span>
</div>
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Listing 2: </span>Pseudo-code for the iterative refinement step</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We replicate the main experiment from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>. We run our algorithm for all pairs of encoders used in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>. Details about the encoders are provided in Table <a href="#A1.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix A Additional Assets ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> in the Appendix. Experiments use k-means clustering from scikit-learn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pedregosa et al., 2011</a>)</cite> and QAP is solved with the scipy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Virtanen et al., 2020</a>)</cite> implementation of 2-OPT. We re-run the 2-OPT alignment algorithm 30 times and choose the permutation with the highest alignment score. This helps improve the robustness of the alignment, as a single 2-OPT is often not enough.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We take a random subset of the Natural Questions dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwiatkowski et al., 2019</a>)</cite> of size <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="60,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>60,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60,000</annotation></semantics></math>, compute sentence embeddings with all encoders, and leave <math id="S4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8192" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8192</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8192</annotation></semantics></math> sentences for evaluation. We split the remaining embeddings equally between the source encoder (space <math id="S4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math>) and target encoder (space <math id="S4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>), so there is no overlap between the source and target sentences. All experiments are run on a Colab notebook with a CPU runtime and repeated three times for each pair to demonstrate the method’s stability. We compare our results to the numbers reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate alignment quality using two primary metrics. The first is <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Top-1 Accuracy</span>, the fraction of queries where the nearest neighbor in the target space is the correct match, defined by:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta(\text{NN}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}_{i})=\mathbf{b}_{i})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Accuracy</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>NN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐖𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta(\text{NN}(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{a}_{i})=\mathbf{b}_{i}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math> is the indicator function, <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{NN}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>NN</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{NN}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is the nearest neighbor of source embedding <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{a}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{a}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> in the target space, and <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{b}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{b}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is its true corresponding target embedding. The second is the <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Average Rank</span>, the mean position of the true match in the sorted list of distances from the query to all targets,</p>
<table id="S4.Ex13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AvgRank}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{rank}(\mathbf{b}_{i}|\mathbf{a}_{i})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>AvgRank</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><mtext>rank</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐛</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐚</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AvgRank}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\text{rank}(\mathbf{b}_{i}|\mathbf{a}_{i}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3" class="ltx_p">We also report the mean <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">cosine similarity</span> after each step of the algorithm to show its progression over the stages. Cosine similarity in itself can be used as an evaluation metric, but it can also be misleading. Cosine similarity in <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> underestimates the similarity in the original space, due to the removal of the mean vector, which is a dominant part of all vectors, accounting for <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 30\%-70\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mrow><mn>30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 30\%-70\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the vector’s norm. Also, setups that move the vectors to a third space, like <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, have an advantage as they can change the geometry. Our setup does not change the geometry (apart from aparametric translation and scaling in the preprocessing step).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hyperparameters</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have found that the method is extremely robust to hyperparameter choices, as long as they are in a reasonable range. For the paper, we made an economical choice of hyperparameter values to shave time for the large number of runs, but we found the choice to be sufficiently robust even still. We use <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s=30</annotation></semantics></math> runs of relative representation alignment with <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=20</annotation></semantics></math> clusters. In the Initial Transformation step, we use <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k=50</annotation></semantics></math> neighbors. We set the sampling rate in Refine-1 to <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{s}=10,000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{s}=10,000</annotation></semantics></math> and utilize <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k^{\prime}=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k^{\prime}=50</annotation></semantics></math> neighbors; In Refine-2, we use <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c^{\prime}=500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>c</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c^{\prime}=500</annotation></semantics></math> clusters. For exponential smoothing, we use <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.5</annotation></semantics></math>.
The full hyperparameter configuration used in the experiments is also documented in the code linked. For the <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textit{gtr}\leftrightarrow\textit{gte}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">gtr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">gte</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textit{gtr}\leftrightarrow\textit{gte}</annotation></semantics></math> pair, we increase the number of clusters to <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=30</annotation></semantics></math>. We find that for this pair, the algorithm often converges to a sub-optimal solution in the <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=20</annotation></semantics></math> regime. A detailed discussion of observations about hyperparameter choice can be found in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Choice of Hyperparameters ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<table id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

Bold indicates best performance. Underline indicates nearly equally good performance (<math id="S4.T1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 0.01</annotation></semantics></math> difference). Bold and underline combined indicate better performance, but only within a <math id="S4.T1.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> margin.
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="S4.T1.7.1" class="ltx_sup">∗</sup> For the <math id="S4.T1.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gtr\leftrightarrow gte" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gtr\leftrightarrow gte</annotation></semantics></math> pair, we modify the number of clusters to <math id="S4.T1.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=30</annotation></semantics></math> in the approximate matching stage.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">From the results in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Hyperparameters ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ mini-vec2vec: Scaling Universal Geometry Alignment with Linear Transformations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we observe that our approach matches or exceeds <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> across (almost) the entire table. The improvement is most noticeable in the rank metric. Importantly, the method is extremely robust as is evidenced by the small standard deviation, already by the end of the first refinement step. Unlike <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, our method does not collapse on the <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textit{e5}\leftrightarrow\textit{gtr}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">e5</mtext><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">gtr</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textit{e5}\leftrightarrow\textit{gtr}</annotation></semantics></math> pair or the <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\textit{gtr}\leftrightarrow\textit{gte}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">gtr</mtext><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">gte</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\textit{gtr}\leftrightarrow\textit{gte}</annotation></semantics></math> pair.
We underline scores that are within a <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> margin, as they might result from rounding noise, stochasticity, and a slightly different experimental setup.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Our results are calculated over multiple runs and a single evaluation set, while vec2vec computes the results of a single run over 8 evaluation sets.</span></span></span> Due to the small variance in most experiments, in both methods, we believe that a <math id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.01</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.01</annotation></semantics></math> margin is good enough.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Analysis</h4>

<div id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The slightly superior results of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> are very encouraging, but even in pairs where the results are slightly worse or match <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span>, the main point is that this is achieved for a fraction of the cost. One run of <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> is completed on a CPU in <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">less than ten minutes</span>, while <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> requires 1–7 days on a GPU, depending on the hardware. Another important point from the point of view of robustness is that even where the <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vec2vec</span> results are relatively low, <span id="S4.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> still performs well, close to perfect performance.
Analyzing the convergence of our algorithm, we observe that despite variation in the Initial Transformation step (Initial), Refine-1 consistently improves cosine similarity and converges to stationary points with nearly identical cosine similarity values across different initializations. This reproducible convergence behavior suggests the optimization landscape is well-structured.
The convergence of Refine-1 appears to reach a stationary point of the implicit nearest-neighbor matching objective. Refine-2 successfully improves upon this converged solution, which might indicate that the converged solution has some systematic bias.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion</h2>

<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Failure Modes</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We find that despite the many experiments we ran, ranging diverse hyperparameter configurations, failure modes were extremely rare. In fact, we didn’t experience <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">any</span> except on the <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="gte\leftrightarrow gtr" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">↔</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">gte\leftrightarrow gtr</annotation></semantics></math> pair, and modifying the number of clusters to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c=30" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c=30</annotation></semantics></math> solved this, though experimentation with more runs has shown that failure modes still exist in the <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gtr</span> <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">gte</span> direction, they are just rarer. Crucially, failure modes are <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not</span> catastrophic. Failure modes are characterized by worse top-1 accuracy and average rank – but the decrease is not catastrophic, leading to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim 90\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim 90\%</annotation></semantics></math> top-1 accuracy and <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5-10" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5-10</annotation></semantics></math> average rank, much better than any naive baseline.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Main Takeaways</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We would like to emphasize the subtle points that make the method work. While word alignment methods weren’t suitable in this setup, they are likely not completely irrelevant. The main drivers of success are stable landmarks and tractable matching. We chose to focus on clusters as these landmarks. However, it is not the only option. A preliminary study <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yamagiwa et al., 2023</a>)</cite> on word and image embeddings has found that Independent Component Analysis (ICA) can identify shared interpretable directions between embedding spaces. We don’t preclude the possibility that they could have been used instead. The important part is to find anchors that are consistent despite zero overlap. This gives us a match between <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sets</span>, and leaves us with the task of aligning the individual anchors. The fact that the number of anchors is relatively small makes the process very fast, but also makes the problem <span id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">simpler</span>. It is easier to find near-optimal solutions when the number of samples is not large, while the problem quickly gets out of hand due to its combinatorial nature. We used QAP for matching, which is closely related to Optimal Transport. The small scale does more than speed up the process, but likely also improves the performance of the algorithm. We believe this might have worked with Gromov-Wasserstein and other OT algorithms as well, as long as the same principles were kept. Last but not least, robustness to noise is another crucial driver of success. While <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf (2018)</a></cite> re-initialize their pipeline (500 times, which is very expensive, though parallelizable) to fight noise and arbitrariness, we use many noisy assignments in one run, addressing the problem without multiple runs. Other tricks, not necessarily common in literature, such as exponentially-smoothed orthogonal matrices, cluster-based matching, and others, have empirically contributed to boosting performance significantly, but even without them performance was decent.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Universality</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The study of universality has its roots in several works. Representation alignment is well-studied in the supervised setup. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lenc and Vedaldi (2015)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al. (2021)</a></cite> have demonstrated that linear transformations are often sufficient for aligning neural network representations in a procedure they called <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">stitching</span>. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mikolov et al. (2013)</a></cite> have identified that word embeddings from different languages converge to similar geometries and used it to align them with a learned linear transformation from a seed dictionary. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Olah (2015)</a></cite> visualized representations from different convolutional neural networks using relative representations. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moschella et al. (2022)</a></cite> have used these insights to transition between representation spaces through a universal space, utilizing it for zero-shot stitching. Concurrently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dar et al. (2023)</a></cite> have demonstrated zero-shot stitching using (a method equivalent to) relative representations with token embedding anchors.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al. (2024)</a></cite> have aggregated and unified previous work under the name <span id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Platonic Representation Hypothesis</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Unsupervised Alignment</h4>

<div id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The task of unsupervised alignment of embeddings, too, has a long history in word embeddings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Conneau et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen and Cardie, 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and machine translation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lample et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. These early methods relied on adversarial training. Artetxe et al. have started a line of supervised and semi-supervised alignment methods relying on an iterative refinement process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, which culminated in VecMap <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Artetxe et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, an unsupervised method that relied on the distributional features of words. Another unsupervised work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hoshen and Wolf, 2018</a>)</cite> used a three-step algorithm not unlike our own, but it required hundreds of re-initializations and used word frequencies. The works of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grave et al. (2019)</a></cite> have utilized variants of optimal transport to align word embeddings. They require the existence of a match between points, at least approximately, in order to work. Works on unsupervised alignment in other domains, for example, image or cross-modal image-text alignment, have mostly focused on semi-supervised setups and overlapping datasets <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schnaus et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Maniparambil et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which inspired our initial attempts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have presented <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span>, a linear approach to unsupervised embedding alignment that achieves competitive performance while offering substantial advantages in computational efficiency, training stability, and interpretability. Our method demonstrates that adversarial training may be unnecessary for reliable embedding alignment, and identifying structural correspondences is possible in other ways. The success of our approach provides another strong empirical evidence for the Universal Geometry hypothesis and suggests that the geometric regularities in learned representations are more robust and accessible than previously assumed. By decomposing the alignment problem into classical optimization components, we achieve both theoretical clarity and practical efficiency.
The efficiency and accessibility of our method can help democratize research on embedding alignment and cross-modal representation learning. By reducing computational barriers, we enable broader participation in this research area and facilitate deployment in resource-constrained environments. From a security perspective, efficient alignment methods raise important considerations about data privacy and intellectual property protection in embedding spaces. If alignment can be performed quickly and reliably, it may become easier to leak data in the scenario described in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jha et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Acknowledgements</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We thank John X. Morris for useful feedback. We thank Google for making CPU and GPU notebooks freely available.</p>
</div>
</section>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A1.T2.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="A1.T2.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Embedding models used in our experiments</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Choice of Hyperparameters</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">mini-vec2vec</span> is stable under different choices of parameters, often converging to similar stationary points. Moreover, unlike many machine learning algorithms, most hyperparameters have a clear interpretation and often have a monotone behavior. Here we share trends that we have observed empirically in some setups, but a rigorous experimental analysis has not been made.</p>
<ul id="A2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of concatenated representations</span>: Increasing the number of runs in the anchor discovery step reduces the number of the failure modes. This is because noisy assignments are diluted, emphasizing the signal from true assignments. Note that even with very few runs, good alignments can be reached at random but with smaller probability.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Number of iterations</span>: We find that the alignment is monotonically increasing as the number of iterations grows, unlike some algorithms where increasing information might cause degradation. This makes it a safe bet to increase the number of iterations. Across all cases examined, though, we found convergence to be quite fast. Almost without exception, 100 iterations were enough by a large margin.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="A2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Subsampling rate</span>: Subsampling allows us to speed up the algorithm quite substantially, but it can increase noise. The larger the sample size is, the closer this approximation is to the data. As a rule of thumb, we generally considered higher sampling rates to be better (at the cost of slower performance), but we haven’t tested this rigorously.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Other hyperparameters are less obvious. <span id="A2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Number of clusters</span> in the approximate matching step is likely good in moderation. While increasing it will give us more landmark points for alignment, it can theoretically lead to instabilities because the assignment of very granular centroids can be noisy. Increasing <span id="A2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">number of neighbors</span> is often beneficial, but it eventually leads to diminishing returns, and might even deteriorate performance when neighborhoods become very large. At moderate scales, it helps to reduce noise, as averaging more neighbors leads to a smoother estimate of the true aligned position. Note that this is more relevant here than in word embeddings, where essentially every point has (more or less) one ground-truth translation and it makes sense to rely on a single neighbor. Increasing the number of neighbors to very large numbers might lead to over-smoothing, which may harm performance.
Finally, increasing the exponential smoothing hyperparameter <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> leads to higher cosine scores, but they don’t necessarily translate to better rank and top-1 scores. <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> is implicitly responsible for the distance of the matrix from being orthogonal. Additionally, increasing <math id="A2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> makes convergence slightly slower.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In summary, unlike many deep learning setups, GANs in particular, the range of hyperparameters that lead to strong performance is generously wide. Each hyperparameter is interpretable, and one can plausibly guess in which direction to modify the parameter to improve effectiveness, if needed.</p>
</div>
</section>
</article>
</div>
</div>
